A1.justification: Both PDFs describe iLLaVA and provide readable text, equations, tables and figures supporting comparison despite substantial revision. All supplied pages were inspected, including v2 Appendix A; v1 contains no appendix.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 report original accuracy, throughput, memory measurements, ablations and document-understanding failure results.

after.justification: Section 4 reports original image/video evaluations, comparisons across compression ratios and model architectures, efficiency measurements and ablations.

M1.justification: V1 merges low-attention tokens into one aggregate using predetermined linear weights. V2 Section 3.2.2 instead selects multiple recycled representatives, groups similar tokens around them and merges using normalized attention weights. LLM merging also changes from one selected layer to multiple blocks. These are substantive algorithm changes.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluations on MMMU-Pro, RealWorldQA and MVBench. It removes substantial coverage, including NoCaps/Flickr30k captioning, AI2D, Q-Bench, SeedBench and several video benchmarks. V1's DocVQA, InfoVQA and ChartQA evaluations disappear; their names remain in v2's limitations without corresponding results.

E2.justification: V2 Tables 1–3 and 6 introduce evaluated comparators including SparseVLM, FasterVLM, PyramidDrop, VisionZip, AdaFV, DivPrune, FEATHER and AIM. FastV and LLaVA-PruMerge remain in Table 6, and ToMe/bipartite matching remains in the strategy ablation. Free-VideoLLM and several earlier ablation comparators are removed.

E3.justification: The default backbone changes from LLaVA-Onevision 7B to Qwen2.5-VL 7B. Encoder layers 3–6 and LLM layer 2 are replaced by a 40/60 merging allocation across encoder layers 5/9/13 and LLM layers 2/8/14. V2 introduces explicit image/video compression grids, normalized performance retention and prefilling latency, changes evaluated model families/sizes, and expands ablation aggregation from three image benchmarks to nine.

E4.justification: V2 adds an explicit LLM-only versus encoder-plus-LLM control in Table 4 and an encoder/LLM allocation sweep in Figure 6. It substantially revises the merging-strategy ablation. V1's separate layer-selection and retained-token-count studies in Tables 5–6 and 8–9 are removed, while the selected-token visualizations are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. V2's normalized scores and benchmark averages are performance summaries, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Much of the result suite is replaced under revised models and compression settings. V2 newly reports 95.2% average image-performance retention at 88.9% reduction and 2.12× throughput/4.46× prefilling speedups; these are not same-setting improvements over v1. V1's quantified document-task losses disappear. Some new percentages are inconsistent: Table 1 reports 57.9 relative to 58.6 as 99.3%, although the ratio is approximately 98.8%.

T1.justification: The mathematical specification changes from v1's single aggregate to informative/recycled token partitions and multiple LLM merging stages. V2 Section 3.3 also introduces an overhead argument of O(Rv)Bv + O(Rt)Bt, replacing v1's O(1) merging claim. Neither version contains substantial theorem or proof development.

C1.justification: Training-free acceleration of both encoder and LLM through information-preserving merging remains the central contribution. The headline claims change from a 0.2–0.5% performance drop and approximately halved memory to over 95% retention across reduction ratios and approximately fourfold faster prefilling. The larger-model-versus-smaller-model advantage is retained with different examples.

C2.justification: V2 Section 4.9 adds an explanation for the 40/60 allocation: excessive encoder compression removes fine-grained spatial information, while moderate encoder reduction also benefits downstream LLM computation. Appendix A.1 retains the document-understanding caveat and adds small-object failures. Moving the existing caveat alone does not constitute a substantive change.

D1.justification: V2 adds implementation information about Flash-Attention, including return_attn_probs and flash_attn_varlen_func, and specifies a typical group size of M = 5. The repository link remains, but the new reproducibility statement describes release as conditional on acceptance, creating ambiguity relative to v1's availability statement. Neither PDF establishes an actual repository-access change.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 is substantially rewritten around newer approaches including SparseVLM, FasterVLM, VisionZip, PyramidDrop, DivPrune, AdaFV and AIM. Earlier discussions of FlexAttention, LOOK-M, ZipVL, HiRED and VidCompress are removed. The research context and comparison landscape change substantially, although the distinction of accelerating both encoder and LLM remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, motivation, method explanation and experimental narrative undergo extensive rewriting and reorganization. V2 separates two-stage merging, merging strategy and efficiency analysis, moves limitations into Appendix A, and adds acknowledgements, ethics, reproducibility and LLM-usage statements.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation. Benchmark tables are reorganized around compression ratios, efficiency plots are substantially redesigned, and an allocation plot is added. The attention illustration changes and its LLM panels disappear. V1 Figures 3 and 6 are substantially retained as v2 Figures 2 and 5.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens support for the central contribution through comparisons across explicit reduction budgets, multiple architectures and an encoder/LLM control, addressing weaknesses in v1's mainly MMMU-centered method comparison. However, it removes quantified document-understanding failures and detailed layer/token-count studies, while reporting inconsistencies remain, including Table 1's retention percentages. These tradeoffs support a limited overall improvement rather than a clear major gain.
